newsitem.title: USA: Penn Traffic bonds drop on weak sales.
newsitem.headline: Penn Traffic bonds drop on weak sales.

text.p: Penn Traffic bonds fell sharply Wednesday morning following the release of negative fourth quarter revenues and same-store sales by the food retailer, high-yield bond traders said.
The company reported a 14 percent drop in fourth quarter revenues and a 6.6 percent decline in January store sales.

"Penn Traffic's 9.625 (percent bonds) fell three points on the news, but are now coming back ... they're quoted at a 33-1/2 bid," said one trader of distressed debt. "Just a couple of weeks ago the bonds were in the high 50's; I don't know that they can go much lower than this."
Penn Traffic's 11.50 percent debt also was quoted off at 82-1/2 bid, down 1-1/2 points from Tuesday, but traders noted the bonds have come up from lows near 78 last month.
Also, Penn Traffic's 8.625 percent bonds were quoted at an 80 bid, off earlier bids of 77 and 79, but the bonds remain off 1/2 point, according to traders.

Several quarters of weak sales, culminating with December's 8.5 percent drop, triggered a tumble in the company's bonds compounded by rumors of bankruptcy and reports of suppliers demanding cash on delivery.

"We continue to have excellent trade relationships with virtually all of our more than 3,500 merchandise vendors, and we maintain virtually all of our trade credit," said Gary Hirsch, chairman of the board, in a press release. "The company's liquidity is excellent."

"While we are not satisfied with our sales in January, the two-year sales trend ... was one of the best of the second half of the fiscal year ended February 1, 1997 and significantly better than December's two-year trend," he said.
In its release, the company said for the fourth quarter ended February 1 (13 weeks), revenues were about $815 million, a drop of 14 percent from the year ago 14-week quarter.

Last month, the company predicted its Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EBITDA) performance would be the highest of any quarter this fiscal year. The company predicted fourth quarter EBITDA between $49 million and $52 million.
"Not until the numbers get better will they be credible," said Sheila McNeely, an analyst with KDP Investment Advisors.

When asked about rumors of a potential Penn Traffic bankruptcy, McNeely replied: "There's a good chance of that happening. The banks need to stay involved; they need to continue to loan money to the company, and the company needs to be able to maintain its covenants but it has continued to break those."
NcNeely noted that the company already has 14 amendments to its bank covenants.
"Hirsch is trying to paint a good face on all of this," said another high-yield bond trader. "There's been constant takeover talk and I think that's what kept up the bonds as long as they have been.
"Hirsch should sell ... he didn't sell Grand Union and look what happend there," the trader added. "He painted a good face on Grand Union for as long as he could, too."
Penn Traffic chief Gary Hirsch, who came from Grand Union, is currently running the company in the absence of a chief executive officer.
((-- Nancy Leinfuss, U.S. Corporate Bond Unit, 212-859-1675))
